If you’ve used Claude Code or Codex and thought

The clearest how-to on building agent loops so far.

@clairevo builds two from scratch in Claude Code and Codex:

A daily loop that reviews aging PRs and schedules itself. A weekly loop that spawns its own subagents to validate its output.

Covers the four loop types, the five things every loop needs, and when each one actually fits.

Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code:

"Almost 100% of our engineers at Anthropic are running 100+ agents with self-improving loops. Self-improving loops help agents get better with each run."

1 hour. He breaks down how they build agent loops from scratch.

Claude plus loops plus routines plus dynamic workflows. That's the actual playbook.

Watch the talk. 

Then read how to apply the exact same system to quant trading below.

A senior Anthropic engineer just dropped an 11-page PDF on "How to make perfect agent loops"

The shift: you stop guessing when the work is done. You build the signal that tells the agent for you.

Run → Score → Compare → Converge → Stop

Every loop runs one cycle, five moves:

• Scoring: each cycle gets a number, tests passing or % complete, instead of a vibe check.

• Comparison: the agent checks this cycle's score against the last one, not just the result in front of it.

• Convergence: once two cycles barely move the number, the work has stabilized. That's the real finish line.

• Restraint: past that point, more cycles cost tokens and add nothing, so it stops.

• Verification: stopping only counts if the result held. Accuracy is checked before the loop calls it done.

The key insight: an agent left to run forever doesn't get more right, it just gets more expensive.

This 11-page PDF changed how I'm engineering agent loops in Claude Code today.

THE CLEAREST BLUEPRINT FOR GIVING YOUR AGENT REAL MEMORY IS FOUR WORDS.

Write. Consolidate. Recall. Apply.

Write: after every attempt, the agent records what it tried and what happened.
Consolidate: it distills the raw attempts into a few reusable lessons, not a transcript dump.
Recall: before the next task, it reads those lessons first.
Apply: it skips the dead ends it already learned, even on a brand new problem.

A broke 23-year-old just made $500,000 with an agentic loop that was too expensive to run a month ago.

Then Claude Sonnet 5 came out, and the cost fell off a cliff.

He'd built the bot last year, in Lisbon, and killed it after a month. The API bills ate everything it made.

Anthropic says it runs on its own at a level that used to take their biggest, priciest models. Running a bot all day used to cost a fortune. Now it barely costs anything.

Here's why the cost was the whole problem.

A real trading bot isn't one question to an AI. It's a loop that runs all day. 

It makes a trade, sees how it went, learns from it, and adjusts. Then it does it again, thousands of times.

Every step costs money. 

On the old models, running that loop nonstop drained your account before it ever figured anything out.

Sonnet 5 runs the same loop for pennies on the dollar.

So now it can run forever, and the longer it runs the better it gets. It keeps what works, drops what doesn't, and rewrites its own rules every night.

Last month that loop cost him about $4000 a day. Now it's under $4. 

That gap is the difference between "not worth it" and $500,000.

Sonnet 5 isn't just smarter. It made running a real loop cheap, and that's what put it in reach of regular people.
